Conversation with Gemini

You said

Application that can copy a Folder Pathway on a VPS (That makes up a Docker Container Data), and periodically backs it up to a Cloud Storage or can transfer it to my Home NAS.


The purpose is that if the data on the VPS is lost, the same Docker application self-hosted on my personal NAS can continue on with a backup resume point.


What solutions are out there for this purpose?

Gemini said

To move your Docker data from a VPS to a home NAS for seamless "resume" points, you need a solution that handles incremental backups (only uploading what changed) and encryption (since it’s crossing the public internet).

Here are the best solutions available in 2026 for this specific workflow.

1. Backrest (The "Docker-First" Choice)

Backrest is a web-based UI for Restic, one of the most reliable backup engines in existence. It was designed specifically to run as a container and manage other containers' data.

  • How it works: You run the Backrest container on your VPS. You map your Docker data folders (the "Folder Pathways") into Backrest as "read-only."

  • The Destination: It can send data directly to S3 (Backblaze B2, AWS), SFTP, or a local path. If your home NAS supports SFTP or MinIO (S3), you can point it there.

  • The "Resume" Edge: It uses deduplication. If you change one small config file in a 10GB folder, it only uploads a few kilobytes.

  • Bonus: It can automatically "pause" your containers during the backup to ensure database integrity.

2. Kopia (The Performance King)

If you want the fastest possible transfers and a very polished UI, Kopia is the current gold standard.

  • How it works: Similar to Backrest, you can run Kopia in a Docker container. It creates "snapshots" of your folders.

  • Connectivity: It has native support for almost every cloud provider and handles unstable VPS connections gracefully.

  • Repository Sync: You can set up a "Kopia Repository" on your home NAS. The VPS "pushes" to it, and if the VPS dies, you simply "connect" your NAS-hosted Kopia instance to that same repository and hit Restore.

3. Autorestic (The "Set and Forget" Scripting)

If you prefer a CLI approach that is easy to manage via a single YAML file, Autorestic is a wrapper for Restic that simplifies everything.

  • The Workflow: You define your "locations" (your Docker folders) and your "backends" (your NAS or Cloud).

  • Cron Integration: It integrates with system cron or can run as a Docker service to perform backups every hour/day.

  • Resume Point: It’s strictly file-based. To resume on your NAS, you just pull the data into the same folder structure and run docker-compose up.

The "Secure Bridge" Strategy

Connecting a VPS to a Home NAS can be tricky due to firewalls and NAT. Instead of opening ports on your home router, use Tailscale.

  1. Install Tailscale on both the VPS and your NAS.

  2. They will see each other as if they are on the same local network (e.g., 100.x.x.x).

  3. In Backrest or Kopia, set the backup destination to your NAS's Tailscale IP address via SFTP.

  4. No ports opened, no hackers invited.

Pro-Tip for "Resuming" the App

To make the transition seamless, ensure your docker-compose.yml file uses relative paths for your volumes (e.g., ./data:/config).

When you back up the entire project folder (the .yml + the data folder), you can literally just copy that whole folder to the NAS and run the same command. The NAS won't even know it's a different machine; it just sees the files exactly where it expects them.

Gemini said

Since you prefer a web-based dashboard, you can narrow your focus to two main contenders that excel at managing remote VPS backups via a browser.

Both of these options run perfectly in Docker, allow you to monitor everything from your laptop, and handle the "resume point" requirement by making restoration simple.

1. Backrest (The Restic "Power User" Dashboard)

Backrest is widely considered the best modern web interface for the Restic backup engine. It’s built specifically to turn the complex Restic CLI into a smooth, visual experience.

  • The Dashboard: You get a clean overview of your backup health, storage usage, and a calendar of past successful runs.

  • Docker Integration: It includes "Hooks." You can tell Backrest to run a command like docker stop my-app before the backup starts and docker start my-app when it's done. This ensures your "resume point" isn't corrupted by an active database.

  • Browsing Files: If you lose data, you can "mount" or browse your snapshots directly in the web UI and click to download or restore specific folders.

  • Setup Tip: Since you use an Asustor NAS, you can point Backrest on your VPS to your NAS's Tailscale IP using the SFTP protocol. This keeps the dashboard accessible and the data transfer encrypted.

2. Kopia (The High-Speed "Native" Web UI)

Kopia doesn't just have a dashboard; the "Kopia Server" mode is a full-featured web app that controls the entire backup engine natively.

  • The Dashboard: It feels like a professional enterprise tool. It’s very fast and gives you granular control over "Policies" (e.g., "Keep 30 daily backups, but only 4 weekly ones").

  • Efficiency: Kopia is generally faster than Restic at "Deduplication." If you have 5 different Docker containers that all use the same base Linux image, Kopia only backs up those system files once, saving you massive amounts of VPS-to-NAS bandwidth.

  • The "Resume" Workflow: On your Asustor NAS, you can run a second instance of Kopia. You simply "Connect" it to the same storage repository your VPS is using. If the VPS goes offline, the NAS instance immediately sees all the snapshots and can restore them to a local folder in seconds.

My Recommendation for Your Setup

Because you are managing multiple Docker containers and want a "resume point," Backrest is likely your winner.

The ability to easily add Pre-Backup and Post-Backup shell commands in the web UI is a killer feature for Docker users. You can stop your containers, run a database export (like pg_dump), back everything up, and restart the containers—all coordinated from the dashboard.

A Quick Security Note: Since these dashboards allow you to delete your backups, do not expose their ports to the open internet. Since you already have Tailscale in your stack, simply bind the dashboard port to the VPS's Tailscale IP. This way, the "Web UI" only exists when you are logged into your private network.
